seo_title: Tile Roof Insurance Appraisal in Texas: How It Works
meta_description: Tile roof insurance appraisal in Texas: why clay and concrete tile claims get disputed, what evidence matters, and fair awards.
h1: Tile Roof Insurance Appraisal in Texas: A Homeowner's Guide
primary_keyword: tile roof insurance appraisal in Texas
excerpt: Clay, concrete and slate tile claims often stall over matching, underlayment and repairability. Here is how tile roof appraisal works in Texas and what evidence moves the award.
key_takeaways: Tile roofs are systems; repairs disturb underlayment, battens and flashing.
Most disputes involve cosmetic vs. functional damage, matching, repairability and hidden underlayment.
Appraisers set the amount of loss but do not decide coverage.
Test lifts, product identification and a detailed estimate are the strongest evidence.
body_html:
A tile roof insurance appraisal in Texas is the policy-based process for settling a disagreement over how much a damaged clay, concrete or slate roof will cost to repair or replace. Each side hires an appraiser, an umpire breaks any tie, and the award sets the amount of loss without a lawsuit.

Tile roofs last for decades, but when hail or wind breaks them, the claim is rarely simple. Carriers and policyholders often look at the same roof and reach very different numbers. This guide explains why tile roof claims turn into disputes, how appraisal works for them in Texas, and what evidence actually moves the number.

Why are tile roof insurance claims so often disputed?

Tile is not a shingle roof with heavier pieces. It is a system: tile, battens or fasteners, underlayment, flashing and trim, all working together. When one part is damaged, the repair usually disturbs the others. That is where most disagreements begin.

Common tile types on Texas homes

  • Concrete tile — the most common tile in Texas subdivisions, heavy and widely available, but colors and profiles change over time.
  • Clay tile — common on Spanish and Mediterranean-style homes in Austin, San Antonio and the Hill Country; more brittle and more expensive.
  • Slate — less common, high value, and very sensitive to foot traffic.
  • Composite or synthetic tile — lighter products that imitate clay or slate, with their own matching issues.

The cost drivers carriers tend to underestimate

A carrier estimate may price "replace 40 tiles" as a modest line item. In reality, a roofer has to remove surrounding tiles to reach the broken ones, protect the field from more breakage, and often source replacement tile from a salvage yard. Each of those steps adds labor and material that a quick estimate can miss.

Cost factorWhy it raises the real cost
Specialized laborTile requires experienced crews; general roofers may not bid it at all.
Detach and resetIntact tiles must be lifted and reset to reach damage, with some breakage expected.
Material availabilityDiscontinued colors and profiles can force larger replacement areas.
UnderlaymentAged underlayment often cannot be patched once it is exposed.
Access and safetySteep pitches and fragile surfaces need extra setup and protection.

The four disputes that drive most tile roof appraisals

1. Cosmetic vs. functional damage

Carriers often classify chips, impact marks and small fractures as cosmetic. A cracked tile, however, can channel water to the underlayment and fail years later. Whether a given fracture affects performance is a technical question, and it is one appraisers regularly address. For the general concept, see our explanation of functional damage in roof claims. Also check whether your policy has a cosmetic damage exclusion endorsement, since that language changes the analysis.

2. Repair vs. replacement

The carrier may approve spot repairs. The policyholder's roofer may say the roof cannot be repaired without breaking more tile than it fixes. Appraisers weigh the repairability evidence, including test removals, breakage rates and the condition of the underlayment.

3. Matching

Older concrete and clay tiles are often discontinued, and even "same" products weather differently. If replacement tiles will not reasonably match, the question becomes how large the replacement area must be. Our guide to matching issues in insurance claims explains how this argument typically unfolds.

4. Hidden underlayment and flashing damage

Tile sheds most water; the underlayment is the real waterproofing layer. Storm-driven displacement, broken fasteners and damaged flashing are hidden from a quick inspection. They show up only when someone lifts tiles and looks.

Tip: Ask your roofer to photograph a few lifted tiles during the inspection, showing the underlayment, battens and fasteners beneath. That evidence often decides whether the scope is a spot repair or a larger replacement.

Texas weather and tile roof damage

Texas tile roofs face a wider range of hazards than almost anywhere in the country. Hail is the most common cause of tile claims, but wind and falling limbs are close behind.

RegionCommon tile threatsTypical claim issue
North Texas (Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano)Large hail, spring supercellsFractures, corner breaks, hidden cracks
Central Texas (Austin, Waco, Round Rock)Hail, straight-line windDisplaced tile, broken ridge and hip caps
Gulf Coast (Houston, Galveston, Corpus Christi)Tropical storms, hurricanesUplift, wind-driven rain, underlayment failure
South Texas (San Antonio, New Braunfels)Hail, wind, heat agingClay tile breakage, matching, brittle underlayment

Hail impacts on concrete tile can produce hairline cracks that are hard to see from the ground or even from a drone. Spalling and corner breaks are more obvious. Wind tends to lift tiles, snap fasteners and break hip and ridge caps, and movement in one area often loosens neighboring courses. If your home is in a hail-prone area such as the Dallas area or San Antonio, tile roof claims are a regular part of the work.

How the tile roof insurance appraisal process works in Texas

Most Texas homeowners policies and commercial property forms include an appraisal clause. When the insurer and policyholder agree there is a covered loss but disagree on the amount, either side can usually demand appraisal in writing. Check your own policy's appraisal clause for the exact wording, deadlines and selection rules.

  1. Written demand. One party invokes appraisal, identifying the disputed claim.
  2. Appraisers selected. Each side names a competent, disinterested appraiser, typically within 20 days under many policy forms.
  3. Umpire selected. The two appraisers agree on an umpire, or a court appoints one if they cannot.
  4. Inspection. The appraisers inspect the roof, often together, and may lift tiles and review underlayment.
  5. Estimates exchanged. Each appraiser prepares or reviews line-item estimates, usually in Xactimate or Symbility.
  6. Agreement or umpire. If the appraisers agree, they sign the award. If not, they submit differences to the umpire; any two signatures set the award.

Under the Texas Supreme Court's decision in State Farm Lloyds v. Johnson (2009), appraisers determine the amount of loss and can consider whether damage was caused by the storm, but they do not decide coverage. That matters for tile roofs, where the line between storm damage and wear is often the core issue. This is general information, not legal advice.

What evidence matters most in a tile roof appraisal?

Appraisal is evidence-driven. The appraiser with the clearer documentation usually has the stronger position. For tile roofs, the most useful items are:

  • Close-up, dated photos of each fracture, with a scale reference and test-square markings.
  • Photos of lifted tiles showing underlayment, battens, fasteners and flashing.
  • Manufacturer and product identification, including attempts to source matching tile.
  • Accurate measurements, including hips, ridges, valleys and pitch. Our roof square calculator helps you sanity-check squares and waste factor.
  • Weather data for the storm date, such as hail reports from the National Weather Service.
  • A detailed line-item estimate that prices detach and reset, breakage allowance and underlayment correctly.

3D documentation can also help. A Matterport capture preserves interior water staining and attic conditions before repairs begin, which supports the link between roof damage and interior loss.

Why ground and drone inspections fall short

Many carrier inspections on tile roofs are done from a ladder, from the ground, or with a drone, partly because adjusters want to avoid breaking tile. That caution is understandable, but it has a cost. Hairline fractures, cracked tile hidden under the overlap, and damaged underlayment are rarely visible in aerial photos. An appraiser who walks the roof properly, or works with a tile roofer who can lift and reset pieces safely, often finds damage the first inspection never recorded. If your claim was adjusted without anyone touching the roof, that alone is a reason to take a closer look at the scope before accepting the number.

Line items often missing from tile roof estimates

When we review carrier estimates on tile roofs, the same gaps appear repeatedly. Reviewing your estimate against this list is a practical first step:

  • Detach and reset of tile surrounding the damaged area.
  • Breakage allowance for tile damaged during removal.
  • Underlayment replacement where tile is lifted.
  • Hip and ridge cap replacement and mortar or foam set.
  • Flashing at walls, chimneys, valleys and penetrations.
  • Steep-pitch and high-roof charges.
  • Code-required items, if ordinance and law coverage applies.
  • Overhead and profit where multiple trades are involved.

For a deeper list across all roof types, see common Xactimate line items missing from roof claims.

Is appraisal the right move for your tile roof claim?

Appraisal tends to make sense when the carrier accepts that there is storm damage but the price or scope is far apart. It is less useful when the carrier denies coverage entirely, because appraisers do not decide coverage questions.

Weigh a few factors before invoking appraisal:

  • Size of the gap. A tile roof dispute is often large enough to justify appraisal costs. Our appraisal cost calculator helps you compare the expected cost to the potential recovery.
  • Quality of evidence. Strong photos, test lifts and a solid estimate improve your position.
  • Timing. Repairs that remove the evidence can weaken the case, so document first.
  • Policy terms. Confirm the appraisal clause, deadlines and any cosmetic damage exclusions.

Appraisal results depend on the facts of each roof. No appraiser can promise a particular outcome, but a well-documented case gives the panel a clear basis for its award.

Next steps for Texas tile roof owners

If your carrier's estimate for a hail- or wind-damaged tile roof does not cover what your roofer says the job requires, start by collecting the estimate, photos and any test-lift evidence. Then compare scope line by line before arguing price.

faqs.q: Does homeowners insurance cover hail damage to a concrete tile roof in Texas?
faqs.a: Most Texas homeowners policies cover sudden hail damage to tile roofs, subject to the deductible and any exclusions. Some policies add a cosmetic damage exclusion that limits payment for dents or marks that do not affect function. Review your declarations page and endorsements, and document fractures carefully so the functional impact of the damage is clear.

faqs.q: Can I get a full tile roof replacement if matching tiles are discontinued?
faqs.a: Possibly. When replacement tiles cannot reasonably match the existing roof in color, profile or appearance, a larger replacement area may be justified. The outcome depends on your policy wording, the visibility of the mismatch and the evidence you present. Documenting your attempts to source matching tile, including supplier responses, strengthens the request.

faqs.q: How long does a tile roof appraisal usually take?
faqs.a: Many residential tile roof appraisals resolve within one to three months after both appraisers are named. Timing depends on how quickly the umpire is chosen, scheduling a joint inspection, whether tiles must be lifted to evaluate underlayment, and how far apart the estimates are. Complex or high-value roofs can take longer.

faqs.q: Who pays for the appraiser in a Texas tile roof dispute?
faqs.a: Under most appraisal clauses, each party pays its own appraiser, and the umpire's fee is split equally between the policyholder and the insurer. Fee structures vary by appraiser, so ask about costs up front and compare them to the size of the disputed amount before invoking appraisal.

faqs.q: Can foot traffic during inspections break tile and affect my claim?
faqs.a: Yes. Walking on clay, concrete or slate tile can crack pieces, and inspectors sometimes cause breakage. Photograph the roof before any inspection, ask inspectors to use proper walking techniques, and note any new breakage afterward. Clear documentation helps separate storm damage from inspection damage during appraisal.
